title: The ages
hookLine: the Granth uses the four ages as a poetic frame for moral decline and renewal

cards: Things were better once. People say it about manners, music, neighbors, prices.

The old Indian world gave that feeling a grand shape: the ages, each darker than the one before, sliding toward the last and hardest, the Kaljug. The Gurus inherited that frame. They didn't throw it away.
But in their hands it stops being a calendar to calculate and becomes something closer to a mirror.

teach.b: First, the word. Jug, or yuga, means an age. The Granth names them: Satjug, Treta, Duapar, and Kaljug, the dark age, the one the hymns place us in.
Second, the chariots. In a salok in Asa di Var, Guru Nanak gives each age a chariot and a driver.

teach.h: A CHARIOT AND A DRIVER FOR EACH AGE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: in Satjug, contentment was the chariot and righteousness the charioteer; in Treta, restraint the chariot and strength the charioteer; in Duapar, austerity the chariot and truth the charioteer; in Kaljug, the fire of craving is the chariot and falsehood holds the reins.
Notice what changes. Not the scenery. The virtues.
Each age is described by what drives people.

teach.h: THE AGES AS A MIRROR OF THE HEART.
teach.b: Third, the mirror. So it reads as poetry about the heart, not a timetable. The Kaljug isn't only out there in history.

It's wherever craving is the vehicle and a lie is steering, and Satjug is wherever contentment carries a life and righteousness guides it. A single day can pass through more than one age. Fourth, renewal.
The Granth doesn't leave the dark age hopeless.
The Japji's very first salok says the True One was true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and will be true.
The ages turn; the True One doesn't. And the hymns point to the Name, and to singing the praise, as what carries a person through a dark age. Decline is real.

how: Sikhs read the Granth's ages, Satjug to Kaljug, as a poetic frame for the state of the heart, and hold that the Name and singing God's praise carry a person through the dark age.

o: a cycle of rebirth from one life to the next
a fixed date when the world is set to end
an age; the Granth's frame for decline and renewal

games.q: the chariots of the ages: tap the pairs.

s: in the Granth the ages are mainly a timetable to calculate
Guru Nanak describes each by what drives people: a mirror of the heart.
the Japji's first salok calls the True One true through the ages
true in the beginning, through the ages, now, and to come.
the Granth leaves the dark age without hope
the hymns point to the Name and singing the praise as the way through.

games.q: in Guru Nanak's salok, the Kaljug has a chariot and a driver. which pair is it?
o: contentment the chariot, righteousness the driver.
the fire of craving the chariot, falsehood the driver.
austerity the chariot, truth the driver.
games.why: the ages are told by their virtues, so the dark age is wherever craving carries and a lie steers.

practice: Think back over the last day or so for a moment when craving was the chariot and something false held the reins: a rush, a grab, a small lie to get by. Just notice it, without scolding.
Then find a moment when contentment carried you and something true was steering, a meal enjoyed, an honest word, and breathe with that one.

wordCard.voice: Jug. An age; the Granth uses the ages, from Satjug to Kaljug, as a poetic frame for decline and renewal, with a chariot and a driver for each. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: ages turn. Both ages can pass through a single life, even a single day. Rest well.
